subtitle: (TUBERCULOSIS / PERSISTENT COUGH)
contentYoruba:

contentEnglish: Materials named in the source: ewu ogan, obu otoyo and black palm-kernel oil. Burn the ewu ogan in a clay pot until it becomes ash. Add obu otoyo in the quantity described in the source, allow the burnt material to cool, then add black palm-kernel oil. The source instructs the person to take one spoonful in the morning and presents it for persistent cough, asthma or tuberculosis.

title: OGUN IGBEBI FUN OBINRIN TO DE ORI IKUNLE
titleOriginal: OGUN IGBEBI FUN OBINRIN TO DE ORI IKUNLE
subtitle: (LABOUR / CHILDBIRTH SUPPORT)
contentYoruba:
Ojo ti agbami ojo ba ro, ao lo si ona oko tabi odo, ao mu igo ofifo tabi
ado ato lowo, ao ri awon ekolo dudu kan, awon miran npe ni kola
tabi olooji, o ni pon to ika, o we lorun bi okoto, ao fi owo lale siwaju
ekolo na, ao fi igo tabi ato yen niwaju re, ao je ko bo sile fun rare, ao
ko opolopo atare le lori, to ba di ehin ojo keje ti obinrin na ba de ori
ikunle ao fun ni mesan tabi mewa ninu atare na, wipe kio je pelu
omi gbona idaji tombila.
contentEnglish: On a day of heavy rain, the source instructs going toward a farm road or river with an empty bottle or container. It describes finding a dark insect/worm called kola or olooji, placing the container in front of it and allowing it to enter by itself, then placing many atare seeds on it. On the seventh day, when the woman reaches labour, the source instructs giving her nine or ten of the atare seeds with about half a tumbler of hot water. This is presented as a traditional childbirth preparation.

title: BI ASE LE LO OYIN IGAN
titleOriginal: BI ASE LE LO OYIN IGAN
subtitle: (USES OF HONEY)
contentYoruba:
Oyin Igan je okan lara ohun ti Olorun da fun lilo wa sugbon opo wa
ko mo bi ase le lo Idi niyi ti ile ise toun lo ewe ati egbo fi so die lara
ona ti a le gba lo Oyin Igan.

ati alubosa funfun pomon ara won. Maa kan si oju mejeji.

2. INU RIRUN; Lo Ewuro po mo Oyin ma lo sibi meji lehin onje ale.

Igan sinu Igo. Agba sibi meji ni igba meta lojumo
M6. AIRI ORUN SU^; Maa mu Oyin Igan sun. Sibi meji lalale.

dudu (STOMACHPAIN) Lo sibi Oyin Merinmerin ni Emerin lojumo.
8 ARONMOLEGUN; Lo Ewuro po mo oyin Igan fi pa ibi ti on ro E. Ki o
lo sibi meji li ojojumo ni owuro kutukutu.

9AKANDUN TABI EEWO(BOIL).
Lo Ewa ati Kaun po mo Oyin Igan. Ma fira ibe.

10. OGBE INU(ULCER);
Maa mu sibi Oyin meta ni owuro kutukutu ni wakati kan ki o to jeun
aaro.
contentEnglish:
The source presents wild honey as a material with many traditional uses and lists ten examples:

1. Eye complaint: mix honey with white onion and apply to both eyes.
2. Internal pain: mix bitter leaf with honey and take two spoonfuls after the evening meal.
3. Wound: mix bitter leaf with honey and apply to the wound.
4. Children’s teething: mix wild honey with lime juice and give one spoonful twice daily after food.
5. Tuberculosis/persistent cough: combine atare, garlic, salt and bitter kola with wild honey in a bottle; the source gives two spoonfuls three times daily.
6. Sleeplessness: take two spoonfuls of honey at night.
7. Menstrual weakness or dark/irregular flow: the source gives repeated spoonfuls of honey daily.
8. Rheumatic pain: mix bitter leaf with wild honey, apply to the painful spot and also take two spoonfuls early in the morning.
9. Boil/akandun: mix beans and kanhun with wild honey and apply to the area.
10. Ulcer: the source gives three spoonfuls of honey early in the morning about one hour before breakfast.

These are reproduced as the source’s traditional claims, not as medically verified treatments.

9. O so pe o le le ejo kuro.

Gbogbo awon nkan wonyi je awon claim inu orisun, kii se eri iwosan ode-oni.

and use the mixture as cream for the child.

Orisun naa so pe ewe guava ni anti-inflammatory, antioxidant ati antibacterial properties, o si gbe e kalẹ fun irora nkan osu ati isun obo.

Eroja:

- Lita omi 1

Ilana:
Se omi lita kan, fi ewe guava kun un, je ki o se lori ina alabọde titi omi yoo fi dinku si idaji. Sokale, je ki o tutu, ki o si fi omi naa fo agbegbe ita obo. Orisun naa ni ki a tun eyi se lemeji lojumo fun ose kan.

The leaves from the guava tree have anti-inflammatory,
antioxidant, and antibacterial properties that have been used for
centuries thanks to their medicinal benefits.
They’re ideal for fighting menstrual cramps and also provide an
excellent solution to the problems associated with excess vaginal
discharge.

Guava leaves have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and
antibacterial properties that have been used since ancient times
for medicinal purposes.

Ingredients
10 guava leaves
1 liter of water

PROCEDURE:
Heat the liter of water and add the guava leaves. Let simmer over
medium heat until the liquid is reduced by half.
Remove from heat and let stand, then rinse the vaginal area with
the liquid.
Repeat this treatment twice a day for a week.

Note:

adopt a healthy lifestyle.
